title: What do A1, A2, B1, B2, C1, and C2 mean?
invitation: Those small level codes appear on books, classes, tests, and language profiles around the world. Here is what they are actually trying to tell you.
summary: Gef uses the CEFR scale as a common way to talk about language ability across languages. The scale is useful, but a level is not a grade, a vocabulary total, or a complete description of a person.

blocks.title: A common map for language ability
blocks.text: A1 through C2 come from the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages, usually called CEFR. It was built so learners, teachers, schools, tests, and publishers could talk about language ability using a shared scale. A and B do not mean school grades. The scale moves from early basic communication through increasingly independent, flexible, and precise language use. Gef uses this scale because the same basic framework can be applied across languages instead of inventing a different progress meter for every language.

blocks.title: Pre-A1 · First steps
blocks.text: Pre-A1 is the space before A1. You may recognize a few words, signs, sounds, names, numbers, or memorized expressions, but you still need substantial support to communicate. This is a real and useful starting point in the modern CEFR Companion Volume, so Gef does not need to invent an A0 level. In Gef, Pre-A1 means you have started learning. It does not mean you have failed to reach the first level. To move toward A1, build a small dependable core for immediate needs, identity, recognition, and very short predictable exchanges.

blocks.title: A1 · Beginner
blocks.text: At A1, you can do useful things with a small amount of language. Familiar topics and concrete situations are your strongest territory. You may understand short simple messages, exchange basic personal information, recognize common words in context, and use simple language to get an immediate need across. Support still matters, and unfamiliar situations can become difficult quickly. Moving toward A2 means making your language less dependent on memorized scripts: add everyday topics, combine familiar pieces in new ways, and become more comfortable with short routine exchanges.

blocks.title: A2 · Everyday
blocks.text: At A2, routine life starts becoming manageable in the language. You can usually get the main meaning from short straightforward material and communicate basic information about familiar people, places, activities, work or school, shopping, travel, time, and immediate needs. You are still working with limited range, but you can do more than repeat prepared lines. Moving toward B1 means connecting ideas across longer stretches of language, handling less predictable situations, explaining simple reasons, and talking or writing about events and plans without needing someone else to carry the whole exchange.

blocks.title: B1 · Independent
blocks.text: B1 is where independent use becomes much more visible. You can manage many ordinary situations without planning every sentence in advance. On familiar subjects, you can follow the central meaning of clear extended language and produce connected communication about experiences, plans, preferences, opinions, and problems. You will still meet gaps and misunderstandings, but they do not end every conversation or text. Moving toward B2 means increasing range, detail, speed, and control so that more complex topics and longer interactions remain workable even when the language is not tailored for a learner.

blocks.title: B2 · Strong independent
blocks.text: At B2, you can take part effectively in sustained communication and deal with substantially more complex language. You can follow and discuss ideas that are concrete or abstract, explain a position in detail, and operate in many social, academic, and professional situations without requiring constant simplification from other people. Errors and gaps still exist, but you have enough range to work around many of them. Moving toward C1 means gaining finer control: inference, nuance, register, organization, style, and the ability to choose language for a particular audience or purpose rather than merely making yourself understood.

blocks.title: C1 · Advanced
blocks.text: At C1, the language becomes a flexible tool rather than a constant obstacle. You can handle demanding material, follow meaning that is not always stated directly, and communicate at length with strong organization and precision. You can adapt to many social, academic, and professional settings and make deliberate choices about tone and style. Moving toward C2 is less about collecting one final set of grammar rules and more about depth: subtle distinctions, rapid reformulation, specialized domains, cultural and stylistic range, and precise control when the language or situation becomes unusually complex.

blocks.title: C2 · Highly proficient
blocks.text: C2 is the highest common CEFR reference level. A C2 user can handle exceptionally demanding language with very fine control of meaning, structure, implication, and style across a broad range of situations. C2 does not mean knowing every word, never making an error, or becoming a native speaker. Languages are too large and varied for that. Experts and lifelong speakers also meet unfamiliar vocabulary and unfamiliar fields. C2 describes an extremely high range of functional proficiency, not perfection and not a new identity.

blocks.title: You do not have to be the same level at every skill
blocks.text: A single level is convenient, but real language ability is uneven. You might read at B1, understand speech at A2, and speak at A1. A heritage speaker might understand family conversations easily while finding formal writing difficult. Another learner may read quickly but freeze in live conversation. None of that is contradictory. CEFR looks at different kinds of language activity, including reception, production, interaction, and mediation. Gef should keep those differences instead of flattening them too early into one number. When Gef shows an overall estimate, the skill profile underneath it still matters.

blocks.title: A book level is about the book
blocks.text: If Gef marks a book A2, that is a reading-difficulty signal. It means the language in the book is intended to be around A2 reading demand. Finishing that book is useful evidence about your reading, but it does not suddenly prove that your speaking, listening, writing, and interaction are also A2. The same rule applies to other materials and tests: always ask what ability was actually measured. A level without its scope can sound more certain than the evidence really is.

blocks.title: The world uses more than one level system
blocks.text: CEFR is not the only language scale. ACTFL commonly uses Novice, Intermediate, Advanced, Superior, and Distinguished ranges in the United States. The U.S. Interagency Language Roundtable uses levels 0 through 5 plus intermediate + levels. Canada uses 12 Canadian Language Benchmarks for English and NCLC levels for French. Japanese learners often meet JLPT levels N5 through N1. Chinese learners meet HSK, which is currently moving through a major 3.0 transition. These systems were built for different purposes, so Gef keeps them distinct instead of pretending every label has one perfect twin in CEFR.

blocks.title: A real example: JLPT and CEFR
blocks.text: Since the December 2025 JLPT, people who pass can receive a CEFR reference level based on their JLPT level and total score. But the official JLPT explanation adds an important limit: JLPT tests language knowledge, reading, and listening, so its CEFR reference does not cover speaking, writing, or interaction. That is exactly how Gef should treat cross-framework mappings. A mapping can be useful without pretending it measures abilities that were never tested.

blocks.title: A framework is not the same thing as a test
blocks.text: CEFR is a framework for describing proficiency. Different exams, schools, and organizations can design assessments and relate their results to CEFR levels. A test score therefore needs its own context: which skills were tested, how the test was linked to the framework, when the mapping was established, and whether the result is official or only an estimate. Gef can estimate progress for learning purposes, but it should never present an app estimate as an official CEFR certification.

blocks.title: There is no universal A2 word count
blocks.text: Vocabulary matters, but CEFR does not define A1, A2, or B1 by one universal number of words. Language-specific researchers create separate reference inventories because languages organize meaning differently. Even the meaning of one ‘word’ changes with segmentation, scripts, compounds, and morphology. An English vocabulary estimate cannot simply be copied onto Japanese, Arabic, Turkish, Mandarin, or every other language. Gef will research vocabulary and grammar targets separately by language, using them as learning guidance rather than pretending they are the definition of the level.

blocks.title: How Gef uses the levels
blocks.text: Gef uses CEFR as the common coordinate system. Books and other content can carry a level plus a skill scope. Your learner profile can keep separate estimates for different skills. A level badge can open this lesson directly at the relevant section. Language-specific curriculum data can then describe which vocabulary concepts, grammar patterns, scripts, pronunciation skills, and text types are useful at that stage. The framework stays universal; the language details do not get translated blindly from English.

blocks.title: How do you move to the next level?
blocks.text: Not by filling one progress bar. Gef should look for repeated evidence that you can handle the kinds of tasks associated with the next level across different material and situations. Vocabulary growth and grammar knowledge can support that evidence, but neither should be a single gate. One easy book should not promote you. One difficult day should not demote you. A strong estimate comes from a pattern: broader understanding, more independent communication, more range, and more control over time. When Gef makes that estimate, it should call it a Gef estimate and show which skills produced it.

blocks.title: The short version
blocks.description: Pre-A1 is your first step. A1 and A2 build basic everyday ability. B1 and B2 mark growing independence. C1 and C2 describe advanced, flexible, precise language use. The code is a useful map, but your real ability is the collection of things you can do.
